# Witherspoon, Other Actresses Push Oscars Red Carpet to #AskHerMore

HOLLYWOOD — Reese Witherspoon was among the actresses at the Oscars who used the red carpet to ask a pointed question of the people holding the microphones: Can we talk about something besides the dress?

Witherspoon joined other women in the industry in urging interviewers to #AskHerMore, a campaign encouraging reporters to steer conversations toward actresses' work, ideas and careers rather than defaulting to who designed their gowns.

Fashion is, of course, a huge part of the appeal of awards night. Millions tune in to see what the nominees wear, and the arrival-line parade of couture has become nearly as anticipated as the trophies themselves. But many women in Hollywood say the focus can be lopsided. They point out that their male counterparts in tuxedos are routinely asked about their craft, their roles and their plans, while actresses field questions about labels and hemlines.

The campaign's supporters say they are not asking anyone to stop caring about clothes. They want the conversation to include more of what they do for a living.

Yet the push raises an awkward complication. In many cases, stars are paid to wear particular designer dresses and to promote the brands that made them. Naming the designer on camera is part of the deal, and fashion houses invest heavily in getting their gowns seen by a worldwide audience.

That leaves a question hanging over the red carpet: can an actress be a walking advertisement for a designer and also insist that interviewers look past the outfit? Some observers argue the two goals can coexist, with a quick nod to the gown followed by a real conversation about a film or a performance. Others say the business arrangements make it hard to change the script.

For now, the hashtag has put red carpet interviewers on notice. Whether the questions actually change may be clearer at the next awards show.

text: Gradual typing combines static and dynamic typing in a single language, letting programmers move between the two styles as a program evolves. The guarantees that make this appealing are enforced by runtime checks, and in many designs those checks carry a cost that is hard to predict. Wrapping values in casts can cause chains of proxies to build up, particularly in recursive or mutually recursive code, leading to unbounded growth in both memory use and running time. This report presents an approach to abstracting gradual typing that addresses these problems while keeping the semantics precise. We start from the Abstracting Gradual Typing methodology, which derives a gradual language from a static one by interpreting gradual types as sets of static types, and we extend it to yield a runtime semantics based on evidence about type consistency instead of ad hoc cast rules. We then show how to represent and combine this evidence so that adjacent checks collapse into a single, bounded-size record. As a result, the space consumed by checks no longer depends on how many times a value crosses a typed boundary. We prove that the resulting language satisfies type safety and the gradual guarantee, and that the compressed evidence is equivalent to the uncompressed form. The report includes the full definitions, auxiliary lemmas and proofs omitted from the conference version, along with discussion of how the design relates to earlier space-efficient calculi.

The first sign was the smell of coffee in the middle of a parking lot.

Maren followed it to a wooden counter that had not existed an hour ago, where a woman in a green apron was apologizing to a man made entirely of black ink. "I just wrote you as the cop," the woman said. "Nobody told me you'd bleed."

All over the city, the pages had spilled out. Detectives from paperbacks stood on street corners squinting at the traffic. A dragon sat on the roof of a bank, bewildered by the lack of a hoard. Someone's cartoon cat was trying to order lunch and had no idea why nobody laughed at his jokes.

By evening, the arguments began. The people from the stories wanted to know who was holding the pen. Maren had no good answer.

"You're all very sure you're real," said the ink man, sitting beside her on the curb. He had stopped bleeding but kept his coat buttoned. "In my story, it always rained. Always. Do you know what it is to want a sunny day and be told no by punctuation?"

"What happens to you now?"

"That's the thing. Nobody knows how this chapter ends." He laughed, which seemed to surprise him. "I have never not known."

Maren thought about her own life, the schedule she hadn't chosen, the plans that kept getting rewritten by strangers. She handed him her umbrella, then felt strange and took it back.

"Come on," she said. "Let's find out together."

Above them the clouds, for the first time, did not seem to be following a script.

Act quickly but calmly. The order below matters, because some steps only work if you do them before others.

**1. Disconnect from the internet**
Unplug the Ethernet cable and turn off Wi-Fi. This cuts off anyone controlling the machine remotely and stops data from leaving. Don't shut the laptop down yet if you want to preserve evidence, though for most home users powering off is fine.

**2. Use a different, clean device for the next steps**
Change passwords from your phone or another computer you trust, not from the compromised laptop. Anything you type on the infected machine could be captured.

**3. Change your passwords and turn on two-factor authentication**
Start with your email, since it can reset everything else. Then do banking, social media, cloud storage and work accounts. Use a password manager to generate unique passwords. Sign out of all active sessions where the service offers that option.

**4. Check your money**
Look at bank and card statements for anything you don't recognize. If you see something, call your bank and consider freezing your credit.

**5. Scan and clean the laptop**
Boot into Safe Mode and run a full scan with a reputable antivirus tool such as Microsoft Defender or Malwarebytes. Remove anything it flags. Check for programs, browser extensions or startup items you didn't install.

**6. If you're unsure, wipe it**
The only way to be certain the machine is clean is to back up your important files (documents and photos only, not programs), erase the drive, and reinstall the operating system from official media. Scan your backups before restoring them.

**7. Update everything**
Install all operating system and software updates, since the attacker probably used a known vulnerability.

**8. Report it if needed**
If your identity or money was involved, report it to your local cybercrime authority (in the US, that's the FTC at IdentityTheft.gov and the FBI's IC3). If it's a work laptop, tell your IT department immediately.

Going forward, keep software updated, use a password manager, and be skeptical of unexpected links and attachments.

Money and Happiness

Many people think money is the key to happiness. Other people think it is not true. I think money is important, but it is not the most important thing.

First, I agree that money can make life easier. When you have enough money, you can buy food, pay for a house, and go to the doctor. If a family has no money, they worry every day. My uncle lost his job two years ago and he was very stressed. He could not sleep well. When he found a new job, he was much more happy. So I think money is necessary for a good life.

But I do not think more and more money always makes people happier. For example, some rich people have big houses and expensive cars, but they are still not happy. They work too much and they have no time for their family. I read about a famous businessman who had everything, but he said he felt alone. This shows that money can not buy love or good friends.

In my opinion, the things that make me happy are not expensive. I feel happy when I eat dinner with my family, when I play basketball with my friends, or when I get a good grade after studying hard. These moments cost very little money. Health is also very important. If you are sick, you can not enjoy anything, even if you have a lot of money.

Also, I think happiness comes from the inside. Some people are always asking for more, so they never feel satisfied. Other people have not much money, but they are thankful for what they have. I think these people are often happier.

In conclusion, money is useful because it gives us safety and comfort. However, it is not the only key to happiness. Good relationships, health, and a positive attitude are more important. I believe the best way is to earn enough money to live comfortably, and then spend our time on the people and things we love.

# Boris Nemtsov Laid to Rest in Moscow as Mourners Say Goodbye to Outspoken Critic

MOSCOW — Boris Nemtsov was buried in a Moscow cemetery on Tuesday after a somber memorial service, as mourners gathered to remember a politician known for speaking bluntly about the Russian government.

Family members, friends and supporters filed past the coffin before the burial. Many came to pay respects to a man they described as unafraid to challenge those in power.

"He always said everything that others were afraid to say," one mourner said, summing up what many in the crowd felt about the opposition figure.

Nemtsov was shot and killed in the Russian capital, a slaying that has shocked critics of the Kremlin and drawn attention from officials and governments abroad. The circumstances of his death remain under investigation.

The Moscow Investigative Committee said "all scenarios" are being considered in the case. The statement did not point to a specific suspect or motive, and it left open the question of whether the killing was connected to Nemtsov's political activity.

For his supporters, the answer seems clear enough, and many in the crowd voiced a mixture of grief and anger. Some stood quietly with flowers. Others spoke in low voices about what his loss meant for the opposition movement and for the few remaining voices willing to criticize the authorities openly.

The service was subdued, with mourners moving slowly and speaking little as they said farewell. After the burial, people lingered at the grave long after the formal proceedings had ended.

Investigators have not said when they expect to announce further findings. In the meantime, friends and colleagues say they intend to keep Nemtsov's memory alive by continuing to say the things he said.

text: We investigate the metallicity distributions of globular cluster systems in galaxies spanning a wide range of luminosity and morphological type. Using published spectroscopic and photometric data, we compile colour and metallicity distributions for the globular cluster populations of early-type and late-type systems and compare their shapes, peaks and widths. We find that the distributions are frequently bimodal in giant ellipticals, with a metal-poor and a metal-rich subpopulation whose relative fractions and mean metallicities vary systematically with host galaxy luminosity and mass. In lower-mass galaxies, the systems tend to be dominated by a single metal-poor population. We examine how the transformation between colour and metallicity can affect the apparent bimodality, and show that its nonlinearity can produce double-peaked colour histograms from smoother underlying metallicity distributions in some cases. We discuss the implications of our results for models of galaxy formation, including major mergers, dissipative collapse and hierarchical accretion of satellites, and consider what the observed trends reveal about the assembly histories of their hosts.

Dolan had never doubted himself until the mirror in the abandoned lab showed him someone else.

He had come to this place to stop the Archivist, the woman who hoarded the city's water supply and rationed it to the poor. It was a righteous mission. He was clear on that. The fires he'd set were meant to force her hand. The guards he'd hurt had been in his way. The bridge he'd collapsed, well, the bridge had been a necessary sacrifice.

Now, standing before her, he saw the photographs pinned to the wall. A boy named Teo, eleven years old, who had been on that bridge. A family from the east district, now living in a tunnel because the market they depended on had burned.

"I kept a list of everyone I've saved," Dolan said quietly. "I used to carry it with me."

"How long is it?" the Archivist asked. She wasn't gloating. She sounded tired.

"Forty-one names."

"And the other list?"

He opened his mouth. He had never written one.

That was the thing, wasn't it? You could be certain of your cause and never once count the cost, because counting would have made you stop. Every decision had felt like courage, and now he wondered whether it had only been the absence of doubt.

He set down the matches. His hands shook, which was strange; they never had before.

"I'm sorry," he said, and it was the first sentence in years that he did not know how to finish.

text:
Cellular respiration is the process by which cells break down nutrients, mainly glucose, to release energy and store it in a usable form called ATP (adenosine triphosphate). ATP powers nearly everything a cell does, from building proteins to contracting muscles and moving molecules across membranes.

The overall reaction can be summarized as: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy. It happens in three main stages.

**1. Glycolysis**
This takes place in the cytoplasm. One glucose molecule (six carbons) is split into two molecules of pyruvate (three carbons each). The process uses a small amount of ATP up front but produces a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH, an electron carrier.

**2. The Krebs cycle (citric acid cycle)**
If oxygen is available, pyruvate enters the mitochondria and is converted to acetyl-CoA. This enters the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix, where it is broken down completely. Carbon dioxide is released as waste, and the cycle generates a little more ATP along with many electron carriers, NADH and FADH2.

**3. Oxidative phosphorylation**
This stage occurs along the inner mitochondrial membrane and produces the most energy. NADH and FADH2 donate electrons to the electron transport chain, a series of protein complexes. As electrons move along the chain, protons are pumped across the membrane, creating a gradient. Protons then flow back through ATP synthase, an enzyme that uses this flow to make ATP. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor, combining with electrons and protons to form water.

In total, one glucose molecule can yield roughly 30 to 32 ATP. Without oxygen, cells rely on fermentation, which regenerates the molecules needed for glycolysis but yields only 2 ATP per glucose. This is why aerobic respiration is so important for the energy demands of complex organisms.

# Tourism: Boon or Burden for Local Communities?

Tourism is one of the largest industries in the world, and it shapes the daily lives of the people who live in popular destinations. Supporters point to jobs and income, while critics highlight crowding, rising prices and cultural erosion. While tourism's problems are real, I believe its benefits generally outweigh them, provided that communities have a say in how it is managed.

The strongest argument in favor of tourism is economic. In many regions, especially those without heavy industry, visitors bring in money that would otherwise be unavailable. Hotels, restaurants, guides, transport companies and craft sellers all depend on travelers. Tourism also tends to create jobs for people with a wide range of skills, from entry-level work to management. For small island nations and rural areas, it can be the difference between a thriving town and one that slowly empties as young people leave for cities. Tourist spending also funds infrastructure such as airports, roads and clean water systems that residents use as well.

Tourism can also encourage communities to protect what makes them special. Entry fees to national parks often pay for conservation, and the value of historic sites gives governments a reason to restore and maintain them. Traditional crafts, music and festivals that might have faded can find a new audience and a new generation of practitioners.

However, the downsides cannot be dismissed. In cities like Venice and Barcelona, residents complain that mass tourism has driven up rents, as homes are turned into short-term rentals. Local shops serving residents are replaced by souvenir stores. Crowds strain public transport and sanitation, and environmental damage, from polluted beaches to trampled trails, can be severe. There is also a risk that culture becomes a performance staged for visitors rather than something people actually live.

Still, these problems are mostly the result of poor management rather than tourism itself. Limits on visitor numbers, taxes that fund local services, restrictions on short-term rentals and policies that keep ownership in local hands can all reduce harm. Several destinations have already shown that such measures work.

In conclusion, tourism brings real economic and cultural benefits, and its harms can be reduced with careful planning. The key is to treat residents as partners, not as scenery.

# New Book Paints a Warmer Portrait of Steve Jobs

CUPERTINO, Calif. — A new book on Apple's late co-founder is drawing praise from some of the people who knew him best, and it offers a softer picture of a man long remembered as demanding and difficult.

"Becoming Steve Jobs" presents a gentler vision of the mercurial chief executive than the one many readers know. Apple executives have publicly praised the book, and some have said they prefer it to Walter Isaacson's 2011 bestseller, which for years has been the standard account of Jobs's life.

Where earlier portraits emphasized his temper, perfectionism and sharp tongue, the new book argues that Jobs grew and changed over time. It traces how a brash young entrepreneur matured into a leader who learned from his setbacks and became more capable of working with others.

Among the book's more striking details is a story from the final stretch of Jobs's life. When Jobs was dying, Apple chief executive Tim Cook offered him a piece of his own liver. The gesture, which speaks to the closeness between the two men, has drawn particular attention from readers and commentators.

The enthusiasm from Apple's leadership has not gone unnoticed. Some observers say the company's executives have a clear interest in how their former boss is remembered, and that their embrace of the new book may reflect a desire to counter the harsher image of Jobs that took hold after Isaacson's biography. Others say the praise simply reflects how closely the book matches their own experiences with him.

Whatever the motive, the book is likely to keep alive a debate that has followed Jobs since his death: how to reconcile the visionary who reshaped consumer technology with the exacting, sometimes unforgiving boss who pushed his colleagues to the limit.

For readers curious about the man behind the black turtleneck, "Becoming Steve Jobs" offers a version of him that is more human, and perhaps more forgiving, than the one that came before.

text: Gravitational microlensing is a powerful method for detecting planets orbiting distant stars, and it is uniquely sensitive to low-mass planets at orbital separations of a few astronomical units, as well as to free-floating planets. Survey telescopes now find thousands of microlensing events each year, but most of these cannot be monitored densely enough to characterise any planetary signal. Follow-up networks of robotic telescopes can fill this gap, though only if observing time is spent on the events with the greatest chance of revealing a planet. We present RoboTAP, a target prioritisation system designed to guide robotic microlensing follow-up observations. RoboTAP takes real-time alerts from survey programmes and computes, for each ongoing event, a figure of merit that reflects the expected sensitivity to planetary perturbations given the event's properties, such as peak magnification, time to peak, impact parameter and source brightness. It combines these with the practical constraints of the observing network, including telescope locations, visibility, weather and the time needed to reach a given photometric precision, to produce a ranked list of targets and a recommended observing cadence. We describe the algorithms used, test them using simulated light curves with injected planetary signals, and demonstrate that prioritised observing strategies recover substantially more planetary detections than uniform sampling for the same amount of telescope time. We also discuss how the system adapts to changes in alerts and conditions, and how it can support future microlensing surveys, in which the efficient use of limited follow-up resources will be essential for measuring the planet frequency in the Galaxy.

text:
The next number is **21**.

This is the **Fibonacci sequence**, in which each term is the sum of the two terms before it:

- 1 + 1 = 2
- 1 + 2 = 3
- 2 + 3 = 5
- 3 + 5 = 8
- 5 + 8 = 13
- 8 + 13 = **21**

Continuing, the sequence goes 21, 34, 55, 89, 144, and so on.

## Where it comes from

The sequence is named after Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, who introduced it to Western Europe in his 1202 book *Liber Abaci*. He described it through a puzzle about the breeding of rabbits: starting with one pair, and assuming each pair produces a new pair every month after maturing, how many pairs would there be after a year? Indian mathematicians had described the pattern centuries earlier, in connection with poetic meter.

## Why it matters

The Fibonacci numbers appear in a surprising number of places:

- **Nature:** The number of petals on many flowers (lilies have 3, buttercups 5, daisies often 34 or 55) and the spiral arrangements of seeds in sunflowers and scales on pine cones often follow Fibonacci numbers.
- **The golden ratio:** If you divide each term by the one before it, the ratios (1, 2, 1.5, 1.67, 1.6, 1.625, 1.615...) settle toward about 1.618, known as the golden ratio, usually written as φ.
- **Computer science:** Fibonacci numbers are a classic example for teaching recursion and dynamic programming, and they show up in some data structures and search algorithms.

## A formula for any term

If you want to skip ahead without adding one by one, there is a closed form called Binet's formula:

F(n) = (φⁿ − ψⁿ) / √5

where φ = (1 + √5) / 2 and ψ = (1 − √5) / 2. Despite the square roots, the result is always a whole number.

For example, F(10) = 55 and F(20) = 6765.

So the answer to your question is 21, followed by 34.

Does Tourism Help or Hurt Local Communities?

Every year, millions of people travel to new places to see famous sights, taste different foods and learn about other cultures. For the people who live in these destinations, tourism can be both a blessing and a headache. In my opinion, the benefits of tourism do outweigh the problems, but only when it is managed carefully.

The biggest benefit of tourism is money. When visitors arrive, they spend money on hotels, meals, souvenirs and tours. This creates jobs for local people, such as waiters, tour guides, drivers and shop owners. In places where there are few other industries, tourism may be the main way families earn a living. Tourism money can also pay for things the whole community uses, like better roads, airports and public transportation.

Tourism can also help protect culture and nature. Many national parks charge entrance fees, and this money is used to protect animals and plants. Old buildings and traditional festivals are often preserved because tourists want to see them. Without visitors, some of these things might be forgotten or even destroyed.

Of course, tourism also causes real problems. Too many tourists can make a place crowded and noisy. In some famous cities, such as Venice in Italy, locals say it is hard to live normal lives because the streets are full of visitors. Rent and prices can go up because hotels and vacation rentals are more profitable than regular housing. Tourism can also hurt the environment through trash, pollution and damage to beaches or hiking trails.

However, I believe these problems can often be solved. Governments can limit how many people visit at one time, charge a tourist tax, or make rules about vacation rentals. Local people should also be included when decisions are made, since they know their communities best. When tourism is planned well, the money it brings can be used to fix the problems it causes.

In conclusion, tourism has both good and bad effects, but I think the good ones are stronger. It creates jobs, supports culture and protects nature. If communities and governments work together, tourism can be a positive force for everyone.

# Iran's Supreme Leader Weighs Legacy as Memory of Khomeini's Painful Peace Lingers

When Iran's first Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, agreed to end the long war with Saddam Hussein's Iraq, he did so reluctantly. He described the decision as bitter, a concession that many in Iran found hard to accept after years of fighting and enormous loss.

More than two decades later, that moment is being revisited as Iran's current Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, faces questions about his own legacy.

Nazila Fathi, a journalist who has covered Iran for years, asks whether Khamenei is trying to put the country on the right track before he dies. Her question speaks to a wider debate inside and outside Iran about how the aging leader will be remembered and what direction the Islamic Republic will take after him.

Khomeini's peace with Iraq stands as one of the most consequential choices of the revolutionary era. Having led his country through a grueling war, he ultimately chose to stop it, even though doing so required him to set aside his own deeply held positions. The comparison is notable because it shows a leader willing to accept a painful compromise for the sake of the country's future.

Whether Khamenei is considering a similar change of course is unclear. Supporters of the government would likely say that he has guided Iran steadily through years of pressure. Critics say the country faces serious economic and political challenges that call for a different approach.

Fathi suggests that the leader's age and place in history may be shaping his choices. If so, the coming months could show whether he intends to leave behind a government that has made peace with its adversaries, or one that holds to the same path.

Either way, the shadow of Khomeini's bitter peace continues to hang over the decisions made in Tehran today.

text: Matrix models and fuzzy spaces provide a framework in which geometry emerges from the dynamics of finite-dimensional matrices. We study how a geometry is encoded in a configuration of Hermitian matrices and how the associated effective actions describe the fluctuations around it. Starting from a set of matrices viewed as quantized embedding functions, we define a Laplace-type operator whose spectrum captures the metric, and we derive the effective action induced by integrating out fields in the corresponding background. We show that this action contains Einstein-Hilbert-type terms, together with higher-order contributions, and we discuss how the coefficients depend on the choice of background. Examples based on fuzzy spheres and related quantized spaces are used to illustrate the general results. We also comment on the relevance of these findings for emergent gravity scenarios arising from Yang-Mills-type matrix models.

Your coworker is right. "Corporate Memphis," also called "Alegria" or "flat design 2.0," is the style of flat, brightly colored illustrations featuring people with tiny heads, oversized limbs and skin in unnatural colors like purple or blue.

**Where it came from**
The name is a nod to the Memphis Group, an Italian design collective from the 1980s known for loud colors and geometric shapes. The modern style is only loosely related, though. Its immediate roots lie in the flat-design movement of the early 2010s, when companies like Apple and Microsoft moved away from textured, three-dimensional icons. Facebook's in-house design team is often credited with popularizing this look, and an illustration system called Alegria, created for Facebook in 2017, helped set the template. Others, including Google and Slack, soon followed.

**Why it spread**
- **It is cheap and quick.** Simple shapes are easy to produce, easy to scale and easy for many designers to replicate consistently.
- **It works across screens.** The vector style looks clean at any size and loads quickly.
- **It feels inoffensive.** Strange proportions and non-realistic skin tones avoid the question of depicting any specific race or identity, which makes the images feel friendly and universal to a global audience.
- **Templates and stock libraries.** Free illustration packs let startups copy the look in minutes.

**The backlash**
Critics say the style is bland, interchangeable and a little condescending, arguing that it makes companies look identical and sidesteps real diversity. As a result, some brands are now returning to more textured, hand-drawn or 3D styles to stand out.

Have you ever looked at a zebra and wondered why it wears pajamas all the time? Scientists have wondered too, and they have a really interesting answer.

Zebras live in Africa, and in many places there are lots of biting flies there. One of the worst is the tsetse fly. These flies bite animals to drink their blood, and their bites hurt. Even worse, they can carry diseases that make animals very sick.

Scientists did many experiments to find out if the stripes help. In one study, they put striped coats on horses. The horses with stripes got bitten much less than horses in plain coats. So the stripes seem to protect the animals!

But how do stripes keep the flies away? Flies have special eyes. When a fly wants to land on an animal, it has to see where it is going. A plain brown or grey animal is easy for a fly to see and land on. But when a fly looks at stripes, its eyes get confused, a bit like when you look at a spinning picture and it makes you dizzy. So the fly cannot land properly and often bumps off or flies away.

Some people used to think stripes help zebras hide from lions or keep them cool in the hot sun. Those ideas might be a little bit true, but the fly story has the strongest proof.

So the next time you see a zebra, remember that its stripes are like a special shield. They help it stay away from bitey flies, and that keeps the zebra healthy and happy!

# Few Close Friends or Many Casual Ones?

Friendship takes many forms, from the person who knows all your secrets to the acquaintance you greet with a wave in the hallway. When asked whether it is better to have a few close friends or many casual ones, I would argue that a small circle of close friends is more valuable, though casual friendships still have a place in a healthy social life.

The main advantage of close friends is depth. A close friend knows your history, understands your moods and can tell when something is wrong before you say a word. These are the people you call after bad news or when you need honest advice. Research on well-being has repeatedly found that the quality of relationships, rather than the quantity, is a better predictor of happiness and even of physical health. Having someone who truly knows you provides a kind of security that a large network of acquaintances cannot.

Close friendships also take time and effort, which is part of why they are meaningful. Everyone has a limited amount of energy for social connection. Spreading it across dozens of people usually means that no single relationship gets enough attention to grow. Anthropologist Robin Dunbar has suggested that people can manage only a handful of truly intimate bonds at any one time, which implies that investing deeply in a few is the more realistic path.

Still, casual friends are not worthless. They widen our view of the world, introduce us to new ideas and can open doors to jobs, hobbies and opportunities. A friendly group at work or in a club makes daily life more pleasant, and these looser ties can sometimes support us in practical ways that close friends cannot.

Even so, when difficulties arrive, it is usually the close friends who stay. A large circle may look impressive, but it is the few people who show up in a crisis who make life feel secure. I would therefore choose a few close friends first, and enjoy casual ones as a pleasant bonus.
